sources.title: Brooklyn Museum, Lukasa (Memory Board), 76.20.4
sources.locator: Object record and publicly indexed museum caption for 76.20.4
sources.supports: The museum identifies this Luba work as a lukasa dated to the late 19th or early 20th century. The caption lists wood, metal and beads and records its dimensions and gift credit.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Lukasa (memory board), 1977.467.3
sources.locator: Public description for a separate Luba memory board
sources.supports: The Met describes Luba memory boards as aids for interpreting and recalling historical knowledge among people with particular training and responsibilities.

sources.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, Tricycle, 1105-0001
sources.locator: Peace Database record 19519, ID Code, Donor, Receiving Date and Description
sources.supports: The museum identifies Shinichi Tetsutani’s tricycle and names his father Nobuo as the donor. It records receiving the tricycle on 6 September 1985 and gives its dimensions.

sources.title: International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, Shinichi’s tricycle
sources.locator: Public article that attributes a remembrance to Shinichi’s father
sources.supports: ICAN connects the object to the Hiroshima bombing and attributes to Shinichi’s father a wish for a peaceful world where children can play.

cases.name: Luba lukasa · 76.20.4
cases.title: The Part That Travels
cases.stake: Nell needs a compact public tag. The host of the reading table has time to walk a visitor through the two sources.
cases.prompt: Put the catalogue details and the public method note in the frame. One face makes the accession easy to carry. The other gives a reader time to follow the separate context source.
cases.dateKind: Approximate period of making in the Brooklyn Museum caption.
cases.alt: Original diagram of a closed wood-coloured mount beside a plain accession slip. No pattern is shown on the mount.
cases.summary: The Brooklyn Museum records this Luba memory board as wood, metal and beads. Its catalogue caption gives 25.4 × 14.6 × 5.7 cm and credits a gift from Marcia and John Friede.
cases.observation: The Brooklyn Museum caption identifies Luba lukasa 76.20.4 and describes what it is made of. A public Met article for a separate specimen describes a role for trained Luba interpreters.
cases.limit: The Met’s article supplies public context about a kind of object. The specific use and interpretations of the Brooklyn board remain with the people and records that can support them.

stamps.name: identity
stamps.label: the Brooklyn caption with the accession
stamps.text: The paper has 76.20.4, the broad making period and the materials. You can send these details with the tag.
stamps.action: Clip the Brooklyn accession and making period to the work order.

stamps.name: context
stamps.label: the separate public note on memory boards
stamps.text: The Met page uses another object, 1977.467.3, to explain that trained Luba interpreters draw on memory boards. Its accession goes on the context note for this display.
stamps.action: Fit the context note in its own sleeve.

variants.control: Put the Brooklyn locator on the outside tag
variants.title: Public locator tag
lines: Luba lukasa. Late 19th or early 20th century. Wood, metal and beads.
Brooklyn Museum 76.20.4. The public context note is at the reading table.
variants.destination: the locator tag by the Gallery aisle
variants.opening: Nell tries the tag during the walk-in queue. A visitor copies 76.20.4 and asks where they can read the separate context note.
variants.action: Turn the tag outward and show the table’s direction.
variants.result: Nell can send a visitor straight to the Brooklyn record. The context note is at the staffed table, where the next group can bring its own questions.

variants.control: Put the two separately sourced lines at the reading table
variants.title: Two-source reading spread
lines: Luba lukasa, Brooklyn Museum 76.20.4. Late 19th or early 20th century.
The Met’s public note discusses trained interpretation through a separate Luba memory board, 1977.467.3.
variants.destination: the two-source spread on the Gallery table
variants.opening: The host makes a second place at the table. “Leave a finger’s width between the two museum names. Both sources belong on the spread.”
variants.action: Open the spread with both accessions visible.
variants.result: The reader matches the board to Brooklyn and the public context to The Met. The aisle keeps a smaller tag that points readers to this table.

cases.journal: I kept Brooklyn 76.20.4 with the object details and Met 1977.467.3 with the public account about trained interpretation.

cases.name: Shinichi Tetsutani’s tricycle · 1105-0001
cases.title: A Name and Two Dates
cases.stake: A reader at the quiet bench wants a name they can remember. The research stand needs both dates with enough room to say what each one dates.
cases.prompt: The family strip and the museum strip have their own places in this frame. Try each first line before carrying a version back to the Gallery.
cases.date: Associated with 6 August 1945. Museum received it on 6 September 1985.
cases.dateKind: Historical event date and museum receiving date. The tricycle’s date of making remains open.
cases.alt: Original simple pixel drawing of a small empty tricycle with three wheels on a neutral background.
cases.summary: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum identifies this as Shinichi Tetsutani’s tricycle. It measures 450 × 475 × 360 mm. The museum names his father Nobuo as the donor.
cases.observation: Peace Database record 19519 identifies object 1105-0001 and gives its receiving date. In a separate public account, ICAN attributes to Nobuo Tetsutani a wish for a peaceful world in which children can play.
cases.limit: The museum supplies the custody entry. The remembrance is Nobuo’s, as reported in ICAN’s public account.

stamps.name: dates
stamps.label: the museum’s two date clips
stamps.text: The first clip marks the Hiroshima bombing on 6 August 1945. The museum’s receipt names Nobuo Tetsutani and records 6 September 1985. Put both labels beside the event they date.
stamps.action: Set the associated event and receiving date on separate clips.

stamps.name: family
stamps.label: the source strip for the public family remembrance
stamps.text: The public ICAN account attributes a wish to Shinichi’s father. He wanted children to grow up able to play in peace. Keep the account’s name with that remembrance.
stamps.action: Set the father’s name and the public account on the family strip.

variants.control: Lead the bench caption with Shinichi’s name
variants.title: Quiet bench caption
lines: Shinichi Tetsutani rode this tricycle. His father Nobuo later gave it to the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum.
The museum connects it to the Hiroshima bombing on 6 August 1945. Museum receipt 6 September 1985, 1105-0001. ICAN’s public account attributes the family remembrance to Nobuo.
variants.destination: the name caption at the quiet Gallery bench
variants.opening: A visitor sits before the doors open. They read Shinichi’s name first and ask how the tricycle reached the museum.
variants.action: Clip the museum receipt behind the name strip and open it for the reader.
variants.result: The visitor follows the donation at their own pace. They copy Nobuo’s name with the account that carries his remembrance. The research stand has a pointer to this bench.

variants.control: Lead the research stand with the two dated events
variants.title: Dated museum record
lines: Hiroshima bombing, 6 August 1945. The museum received object 1105-0001 on 6 September 1985.
Shinichi Tetsutani’s tricycle. His father Nobuo was the donor. ICAN’s public account attributes the family remembrance to him.
variants.destination: the dated tricycle caption at the Gallery research stand
variants.opening: Two readers put the date clips side by side. One points to the receipt. “Here is where the tricycle enters the museum record. Keep the names beside both dates.”
variants.action: Seat both clips and fasten the family strip alongside.
variants.result: Readers can trace the change in custody and keep both names in view. The quiet bench has a smaller card that leads to the full entry.

cases.journal: I kept the Hiroshima event and the museum receipt as separate dates. I credited the museum’s record and the public account that attributes the family remembrance.
